The tag of `LOG.tag(...)` is passed as an SLF4J `Marker` of that name, so `%marker` of Logback prints it and the filters of the backend can select on it.
- The pairs of `LOG.context(...)` are put into the MDC while an entry is forwarded and taken out afterwards; values the MDC already held for those keys are put back. Backends that support MDC (Logback and Log4j 2) print them through their own patterns such as `%X{requestId}`, like values set through `org.slf4j.MDC`; slf4j-simple and slf4j-nop silently discard them, and the JUL binding (slf4j-jdk14) stores them without printing.
- An entry without a message is passed with an empty message, not the word `null`.
- An entry without a source class goes to the SLF4J `ROOT` logger.
- Loggers are cached per source class in a `ConcurrentHashMap` and never evicted, so with dynamic class reloading the cache retains `Class` references.

### JulLogger

*Since 1.4.*

Writes the entries to `java.util.logging`, for an application that configures its logging there, with no SLF4J and no binding:

```properties
nanolog.logger=com.nanolaba.logging.JulLogger
```

- Each entry goes to the JUL logger named after its source class. JUL decides the levels (`logging.properties`), and `LOG.isDebugEnabled()` asks it. `TRACE`, `DEBUG`, `INFO`, `WARN` and `ERROR` become `FINEST`, `FINE`, `INFO`, `WARNING` and `SEVERE`, so `LOG.dbg` is a `FINE` record.
- The message arrives formatted, followed by the fields of `LOG.kv` and the context as `key=value`, since JUL has no place for them; the record names the call site as its source class and method, which `%2$s` of `SimpleFormatter` prints.
- On the module path the application needs the module `java.logging`.

### MemoryLogger and CompositeLogger

`MemoryLogger` keeps entries in memory for tests. Every level is enabled, so entries are captured whatever the production configuration says, and nothing is printed.

```java
void chargeIsRetried() {
    try (MemoryLogger log = MemoryLogger.install()) { // close() puts the previous logger back
        new PaymentService().charge(42); // the code under test

        log.assertLogged(LogEntry.LogEntryLevel.WARN, "Charge of 42 failed, retrying");
        log.assertNoneAtOrAbove(LogEntry.LogEntryLevel.ERROR); // a failure lists everything that was logged
    }
}
```

- `install()` replaces the logger of `LOG` and remembers the previous one; `close()` puts it back, even when the test fails. `installForwarding()` does the same but still passes every entry to the previous logger, so the usual output stays visible.
- `getEntries()`, `getEntries(level)`, `getEntries(SomeClass.class)`, `getMessages()`, `contains(level, text)`, `clear()` — snapshots and short assertions; the logger is thread-safe.
- `assertNoneAtOrAbove(WARN)`, `assertLogged(level, text)`, `assertTemplateLogged(level, "Retry {} of {}")` — assertions that throw `AssertionError` without JUnit or AssertJ. The message lists every captured entry with its call site and stack trace, so the failing test shows what was logged without a second run. `assertNoneAtOrAbove(WARN)` checks that the code logged no warning and no error; `assertTemplateLogged` matches the message before its arguments were substituted.
- `new MemoryLogger(capacity)` keeps only the newest entries.
- `LOG.init` and `install()` are JVM-wide, so tests that install a logger must not run in parallel with each other. For parallel tests use `capture()`, below.

Since 1.4, `capture()` keeps the entries of the current thread only, so tests that JUnit runs in parallel in one JVM each see their own, while the logger of `LOG` stays installed for the others:

```java
void chargeIsRetriedInParallel() { // safe while JUnit runs other tests in parallel
    try (MemoryLogger log = MemoryLogger.capture()) { // this thread only; the logger of LOG stays installed
        new PaymentService().charge(42);

        log.assertLogged(LogEntry.LogEntryLevel.WARN, "Charge of 42 failed, retrying");
    }
}
```

- The capture takes every level, whatever the levels of the logger. The entries of this thread do not reach that logger, though a logger installed while the capture is open, `MemoryLogger.install()` for one, receives them; `captureForwarding()` passes them on as well, at the levels the logger has enabled. The findings of strict mode and of `nanolog.dbg=fail` on this thread go to the capture too, for `assertNoDiagnostics()`.
- Only the current thread is captured: entries that the code under test logs from a thread pool reach the logger of `LOG`. Captures nest, and `close()` may run on any thread.
- Without an open capture logging reads one counter and nothing else of the captures.

`CompositeLogger` sends every entry to several loggers. Each of them receives only the levels it has enabled, and a lazy message is built only if at least one of them wants it. A logger that throws is reported once with a `[NANOLOG]` line and skipped; the others still receive the entry:

```java
MemoryLogger memory = new MemoryLogger(1000); // keeps the newest 1000 entries
LOG.init(new CompositeLogger(memory, new ConsoleLogger()));
```

## Logs in tests: only the failing ones

*Since 1.4.*

The log of a passing test is noise; the log of a failing one is the evidence. A Spring Boot test suite can print thousands of lines per green run, and the agent, or the person, reading it cannot find the failure in them. `NanologExtension` holds back what each test writes and prints it only when the test fails.

```java
@ExtendWith(NanologExtension.class)
class PaymentServiceTest {

    @Test
    void chargeIsRetried() { ... }
}
```

```
--- log of PaymentServiceTest.chargeIsRetried ---
INFO 17.11.2026 10:15:02 [PaymentService] Charging order 17
WARN 17.11.2026 10:15:02 [PaymentService] Charge of 42 failed, retrying
--- end of the log of PaymentServiceTest.chargeIsRetried ---
```

- **What is held back.** What the thread of the test writes to the logger of `LOG`, at the levels of that logger, from the `@BeforeEach` methods to the `@AfterEach` ones. When the test fails, it is written to that logger after all, between the two lines above; when it passes or is aborted, it goes only to the [run log](#run-log), if that is on. A failed test that logged nothing prints nothing.
- **Parallel tests.** Each test holds back the entries of its own thread, so tests that JUnit runs in parallel keep their logs apart. Entries that the code under test logs from a thread pool are not held back.
- **MemoryLogger works as usual.** A test that installs a `MemoryLogger` or opens `MemoryLogger.capture()` sees its entries; see [MemoryLogger and CompositeLogger](#memorylogger-and-compositelogger).
- **Settings.** `nanolog.junit.output` (`NANOLOG_JUNIT_OUTPUT`): `failed`, the default, `all` (every log, as it is written) or `none`. With `junit.jupiter.extensions.autodetection.enabled=true` in `junit-platform.properties` JUnit registers the extension for every test class, without `@ExtendWith`.
- **No dependency.** The extension is compiled against the JUnit Jupiter API, which the tests have anyway; **Nanolog** itself still has none.

## Message formatting

```java
LOG.info("User {} logged in from {}", "alice", "10.0.0.1");  // User alice logged in from 10.0.0.1
LOG.info("Missing arguments stay as is: {} {}", 1);          // Missing arguments stay as is: 1 {}
LOG.info("Extra arguments are ignored: {}", 1, 2);           // Extra arguments are ignored: 1
LOG.info("Escaped placeholder: \\{} then {}", 1);           // Escaped placeholder: {} then 1
LOG.info("Escaped backslash: \\\\{}", 1);                  // Escaped backslash: \1
LOG.info("Arrays: {} and {}", new int[]{1, 2}, new String[][]{{"a"}, {"b"}}); // Arrays: [1, 2] and [[a], [b]]
LOG.info("Null is fine: {}", (Object) null);                 // Null is fine: null
LOG.info("Broken toString(): {}", new BrokenToString());     // Broken toString(): [FAILED toString()]
LOG.error("Failed to load {}", "order", new IOException("timeout")); // Failed to load order, then the stack trace
LOG.error("Cause: {}", new IOException("timeout"));          // Cause: java.io.IOException: timeout
```

- `{}` is replaced by the next argument; `\{}` is a literal `{}` and consumes no argument; `\\{}` is a literal backslash followed by a substitution.
- A `Throwable` in the last position that no `{}` consumes is not an argument: it becomes the exception of the entry, and its stack trace is logged, as in SLF4J. In `LOG.error("Cause: {}", e)` the placeholder takes the exception, so only `e.toString()` is printed. An exception passed first always wins; a trailing one then stays an ordinary argument.
- Primitive arrays are rendered with `Arrays.toString`, object arrays with `Arrays.deepToString`.
- Every `toString()` is guarded: if it throws, the value becomes `[FAILED toString()]` and nothing propagates to the caller. A throwable whose stack trace cannot be printed becomes `[FAILED printStackTrace()]`.
- A lazy message is guarded the same way: if its `Supplier` throws, the entry is still logged, with the message `[FAILED supplier: <exception>]`, for example `[FAILED supplier: java.lang.IllegalStateException: no report]`; the exception and the arguments of the entry are kept. The supplier runs at most once.
- `LOG.lazy(supplier)` makes one argument lazy: `LOG.debug("Stats: {}", LOG.lazy(() -> summarize(stats)))` computes the value only if the level is enabled and only once, however many loggers format the entry. Unlike a lazy message, the template stays a template for strict mode, for the `template` and `args` of `JsonLogger` and for `assertTemplateLogged`, and no `isDebugEnabled()` check is needed. A supplier that throws gives `[FAILED supplier: <exception>]` in place of the value. There are no overloads that take a `Supplier` for the arguments: they would make calls ambiguous, from Kotlin as well.
- The message object itself may be anything, not only a `String`; it is converted with the same guarded `toString()`.
- With `nanolog.dump=auto` (`NANOLOG_DUMP=auto`) an argument whose class has no `toString()` of its own is printed field by field, as in [`LOG.dbg`](#objects-without-tostring): `LOG.info("Added {}", line)` prints `Added Line{sku="A-1", qty=2}` instead of `Added Line@1e643faf`. Collections, maps, arrays and `Optional` are walked, so a list of such objects is printed the same way. Everything with a `toString()` of its own, strings included, prints as before, without quotes, limits or redaction. The setting is off by default because it changes existing output; `JsonLogger` puts the result into `message` and `args` as text. Since 1.4.

### Fields: named arguments

*Since 1.4.*

`LOG.kv(key, value)` names an argument, so that a script or an agent can select the entry by it instead of matching the text of the message:

```java
LOG.info("Loaded {} items from {}", LOG.kv("count", count), LOG.kv("source", source));
// INFO 16.11.2026 10:15:02 [Importer] Loaded 3 items from db
// JSON: "message":"Loaded 3 items from db",...,"fields":{"count":3,"source":"db"}

LOG.info("Payment accepted", LOG.kv("orderId", orderId));
// INFO 16.11.2026 10:15:02 [PaymentService] Payment accepted orderId=A-17
// JSON: "message":"Payment accepted","fields":{"orderId":"A-17"}

LOG.error("Payment failed", LOG.kv("orderId", orderId), e); // the exception goes last
```

- In a `{}` a field prints its value like any argument, so existing messages keep their text.
- A field that no `{}` takes is not an extra argument: `ConsoleLogger` and `Slf4jLogger` append it as `key=value`, quoted like the pairs of the [context](#context-tag-the-lines-of-one-request), and strict mode does not report it.
- `JsonLogger` writes every field into `"fields"`, whether a `{}` took it or not; numbers and booleans stay JSON numbers and booleans. Any logger reads them from `LogEntry.getFields()`, and those the message does not show from `getTrailingFields()`.
- An exception goes last, after the fields, and becomes the exception of the entry as usual. A key given twice keeps its last value; `LOG.kv(null, value)` is a plain argument.
- Names inside the braces, `{orderId}`, are not supported: `{word}` is ordinary text in existing messages.

### Checking placeholders in tests

Leniency about `{}` is right in production, but during development it hides mistakes: a dropped argument
leaves no trace in the output at all. With `nanolog.strict=true` (or `NANOLOG_STRICT=true`), every call
with arguments whose number of `{}` placeholders differs from the number of arguments additionally
prints one line with the call site to `System.err`:

```
[NANOLOG] com.acme.PaymentService.charge(PaymentService.java:87): 2 placeholders, 1 argument in "Charge of {} for {}"
```

Two more mistakes are reported the same way, with the call site:

```
[NANOLOG] com.acme.PaymentService.charge(PaymentService.java:91): argument 1 repeats the message of the exception
[NANOLOG] com.acme.LoginService.login(LoginService.java:40): the template is not a constant: "User 17 logged in from {}"
```

- An argument that is the message of the exception logged with it, as in `LOG.error("Charge failed: {}", e.getMessage(), e)`: the stack trace prints the message already. Name what failed instead: `LOG.error("Charge of {} failed", orderId, e)`. Only the string that `getMessage()` returns counts, and an exception without a message is not checked.
- A call site seen with two templates, as in `LOG.info("User " + id + " logged in from {}", ip)`: a template built from data groups nothing, since the `template` of `JsonLogger` and `assertTemplateLogged` see a new one every time. Put the value into a `{}`: `LOG.info("User {} logged in from {}", id, ip)`. The first template of each call site is remembered. Calls without arguments, such as `LOG.info(report)`, and calls with an explicit class are not checked. A call site is a line, so two calls on one line count as one, and a template chosen by `?:` between two constants is reported too.

For all three checks:

- The entry itself is logged exactly as without the check, and nothing is thrown.
- Each finding is printed once; the 1000 most recent printed findings are remembered.
- Only calls with arguments and enabled levels are checked. Escaped `\{}` does not count, and a trailing exception taken as the exception of the entry is not an argument.
- When the check is off, it costs one boolean test per call. The setting is read by `LOG.init()`.

Turn it on for test runs, so mismatches show up in the output that is read anyway:

```xml
<plugin>
    <artifactId>maven-surefire-plugin</artifactId>
    <configuration>
        <systemPropertyVariables>
            <nanolog.strict>true</nanolog.strict>
        </systemPropertyVariables>
    </configuration>
</plugin>
```

```groovy
test {
    systemProperty 'nanolog.strict', 'true'
}
```

A line on standard error is easy to miss among thousands; `MemoryLogger` turns it into a failing test. Strict mode hands every finding to the installed logger as well (`ILogger.onDiagnostic`), every occurrence and not only the first one of a template, so a test fails even when an earlier test met the same mismatch:

```java
void noPlaceholderMismatches() { // the test run sets -Dnanolog.strict=true
    try (MemoryLogger log = MemoryLogger.install()) {
        new PaymentService().charge(42);

        log.assertNoDiagnostics(); // fails with the call site and the template of every mismatch
    }
}
```

- `getDiagnostics()` returns the findings, `assertNoDiagnostics()` fails with all of them in the message; `clear()` drops them together with the entries. `CompositeLogger` passes them to its delegates.
- Without strict mode there is nothing to report and `assertNoDiagnostics()` passes, so switch it on for the test run as above.
- `nanolog.dbg=fail` reports `LOG.dbg` calls the same way, see [Leftover calls](#leftover-calls).

## Logging payloads safely

*Since 1.4.*

Prompts and responses of a language model, request bodies and documents are either not logged at all or logged raw, keys pasted into them included. `LOG.content(value)` is the middle ground: the text in development, a summary in production.

```java
LOG.debug("Prompt to {}: {}", model, LOG.content(prompt));
// by default:                     Prompt to gpt-x: [content 1834 chars #3f2a9c1b]
// -Dnanolog.content=truncate:20:  Prompt to gpt-x: You are a helpful as... [+1814 chars]
// -Dnanolog.content=show:         Prompt to gpt-x: You are a helpful assistant.\nAnswer briefly. ...

LOG.info("Answer received", LOG.kv("answer", LOG.content(answer)), LOG.kv("tokens", 812));
// JSON: "fields":{"answer":{"content_len":5120,"content_hash":"9c41d2e7"},"tokens":812}
```

- **By default** a payload is its length and a hash of eight hexadecimal digits. Equal payloads have equal hashes within a run, so a repeated prompt or a retry is recognised without its text; the hash is keyed with a random key of the JVM, so the log does not reveal a short payload, such as a pasted key, to someone who tries candidates. Java AI frameworks keep prompt content out of the logs by default for the same reason, and the logs a coding agent reads are sent to its model provider.
- **`nanolog.content`** (`NANOLOG_CONTENT`) is `hide`, `truncate:<characters>` or `show`, and `nanolog.content.<package or class>` sets it for one package or class, the most specific rule winning, as with levels: `-Dnanolog.content.com.acme.llm=show` shows the prompts of one package while you debug. Rules for packages are system properties or keys of `nanolog.properties`.
- **Escaped.** In the text that reaches the log, line breaks and control characters are escaped, `\n` and `\u001b`, so a pasted payload cannot forge a log line; a tab stays.
- **Taken once.** The text is taken when the entry is created, with the guarded `toString()` of a `{}` argument, so a payload that changes later or breaks its `toString()` changes nothing. A payload in a `LOG.context(...)` is taken for each entry and follows the rule of the class of that entry.
- **JSON.** In `"fields"` and `"context"` a hidden payload is `{"content_len":1834,"content_hash":"3f2a9c1b"}`; `message` and `args` hold the text as the console writes it.
- **Known keys are masked.** A shown or truncated payload has keys of model providers (`sk-...`), AWS access keys (`AKIA...`), bearer tokens and JSON web tokens replaced by `sk-***`, `AKIA***`, `Bearer ***` and `eyJ***`. Other secrets inside it, such as a password in plain words, are written as they are; only payloads are scanned, never the text of messages.

## Masking secrets

*Since 1.4.*

Tokens and passwords reach the log through `{}` arguments, fields and the context, and the logs a coding agent reads are sent to its model provider. `LOG.secret(value)` marks a secret, and fields and context named like secrets are masked without it:

```java
LOG.info("Login of {} with {}", user, LOG.secret(token));
// INFO 16.11.2026 10:15:02 [AuthService] Login of alice with ***

LOG.info("Connected", LOG.kv("url", url), LOG.kv("password", password));
// INFO 16.11.2026 10:15:02 [Database] Connected url=jdbc:postgresql://db/shop password=***
```

- `LOG.secret` keeps no value and never formats it, so its `toString()` is not called; every logger writes `***`, in the message, in `args` and `fields` of `JsonLogger`, in the MDC of `Slf4jLogger` and in the assertion messages of `MemoryLogger`.
- A field of `LOG.kv(...)` or a value of `LOG.context(...)` is masked when its key, or a word of it, is in `nanolog.redact` (`NANOLOG_REDACT`): by default `password`, `passwd`, `secret`, `token`, `apikey`, `credential` and `authorization`. Words are split at separators and at camel case, so `password` covers `db.password` and `userPassword`, and `token` covers `X-Auth-Token` but not `input_tokens`. The value is masked when the entry is created, so a `{}` that takes the field shows `***` too. A list replaces the default one; an empty value turns masking off.
- The text of messages is not scanned: scanning every message is slow and gives a false sense of safety. Payloads of [`LOG.content`](#logging-payloads-safely) have the known key formats masked when they are shown.

## Logging LLM calls

*Since 1.4.*

Spring AI and LangChain4j have switches that log requests and responses, but they print `toString()` dumps and pretty-printed JSON. A listener or an advisor of about twenty lines logs one line per call through Nanolog instead: the model, the tokens, the latency and the finish reason, under the field names of the [OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions](https://github.com/open-telemetry/semantic-conventions-genai) (the `gen_ai.client.inference` span, status Development in November 2026). The prompt and the completion go through [`LOG.content`](#logging-payloads-safely), and at `DEBUG` so does a short transcript.

> [!NOTE]
> These snippets are not compiled by the build of Nanolog, which targets Java 8, while both frameworks need Java 17. They are written against LangChain4j 1.x and Spring AI 2.0.

### LangChain4j

A `ChatModelListener`, registered with `.listeners(List.of(new NanologChatListener()))` on the builder of the model:

```java
public class NanologChatListener implements ChatModelListener {

    @Override
    public void onRequest(ChatModelRequestContext context) {
        context.attributes().put("nanolog.start", System.nanoTime());
        if (LOG.isDebugEnabled()) {
            LOG.debug("chat request {}", LOG.content(transcript(context.chatRequest().messages())));
        }
    }

    @Override
    public void onResponse(ChatModelResponseContext context) {
        ChatResponseMetadata metadata = context.chatResponse().metadata();
        TokenUsage usage = metadata.tokenUsage();
        long start = (Long) context.attributes().get("nanolog.start");
        LOG.info("chat {} {} ms",
                 LOG.kv("gen_ai.request.model", context.chatRequest().parameters().modelName()),
                 LOG.kv("duration_ms", (System.nanoTime() - start) / 1_000_000),
                 LOG.kv("gen_ai.provider.name", context.modelProvider()),
                 LOG.kv("gen_ai.response.model", metadata.modelName()),
                 LOG.kv("gen_ai.usage.input_tokens", usage == null ? null : usage.inputTokenCount()),
                 LOG.kv("gen_ai.usage.output_tokens", usage == null ? null : usage.outputTokenCount()),
                 LOG.kv("gen_ai.response.finish_reasons", metadata.finishReason()),
                 LOG.kv("gen_ai.output.messages", LOG.content(context.chatResponse().aiMessage().text())));
    }

    @Override
    public void onError(ChatModelErrorContext context) {
        LOG.error(context.error(), "chat {} failed",
                  LOG.kv("gen_ai.request.model", context.chatRequest().parameters().modelName()));
    }

    private static String transcript(List<ChatMessage> messages) {
        StringBuilder out = new StringBuilder();
        for (ChatMessage message : messages) {
            String text = message instanceof SystemMessage s ? s.text()
                        : message instanceof UserMessage u && u.hasSingleText() ? u.singleText()
                        : message instanceof AiMessage a ? a.text()
                        : message instanceof ToolExecutionResultMessage t ? t.text()
                        : String.valueOf(message);
            out.append('[').append(message.type()).append("] ").append(text).append('\n');
        }
        return out.toString();
    }
}
```

```
INFO [NanologChatListener] chat gpt-4o-mini 812 ms gen_ai.provider.name=OPEN_AI gen_ai.response.model=gpt-4o-mini-2024-07-18 gen_ai.usage.input_tokens=1834 gen_ai.usage.output_tokens=212 gen_ai.response.finish_reasons=STOP gen_ai.output.messages="[content 980 chars #9c41d2e7]"
```

### Spring AI

A `CallAdvisor`, registered with `ChatClient.builder(chatModel).defaultAdvisors(new NanologAdvisor())`. It makes each call a [unit of work](#wide-events-one-line-per-request-canonical-log-lines), so the line gets the outcome and the latency, and a thrown exception is attached to it:

```java
public class NanologAdvisor implements CallAdvisor {

    @Override
    public String getName() {
        return "NanologAdvisor";
    }

    @Override
    public int getOrder() {
        return Ordered.LOWEST_PRECEDENCE; // the last advisor, next to the model
    }

    @Override
    public ChatClientResponse adviseCall(ChatClientRequest request, CallAdvisorChain chain) {
        Prompt prompt = request.prompt();
        if (LOG.isDebugEnabled()) {
            LOG.debug("chat request {}", LOG.content(transcript(prompt.getInstructions())));
        }
        LOG.Unit unit = LOG.unit("chat")
                           .put("gen_ai.request.model", prompt.getOptions() == null ? null : prompt.getOptions().getModel());
        return unit.run(() -> {
            ChatClientResponse response = chain.nextCall(request);
            ChatResponse chat = response.chatResponse();
            if (chat != null) {
                ChatResponseMetadata metadata = chat.getMetadata();
                Generation result = chat.getResult();
                unit.put("gen_ai.response.model", metadata.getModel())
                    .put("gen_ai.response.id", metadata.getId())
                    .put("gen_ai.usage.input_tokens", metadata.getUsage().getPromptTokens())
                    .put("gen_ai.usage.output_tokens", metadata.getUsage().getCompletionTokens())
                    .put("gen_ai.response.finish_reasons", result == null ? null : result.getMetadata().getFinishReason())
                    .put("gen_ai.output.messages", LOG.content(result == null ? null : result.getOutput().getText()));
            }
            return response;
        });
    }

    private static String transcript(List<Message> messages) {
        StringBuilder out = new StringBuilder();
        for (Message message : messages) {
            out.append('[').append(message.getMessageType()).append("] ").append(message.getText()).append('\n');
        }
        return out.toString();
    }
}
```

```
INFO [NanologAdvisor] chat ok 812 ms parent=agent-turn gen_ai.request.model=gpt-4o-mini gen_ai.response.model=gpt-4o-mini-2024-07-18 gen_ai.response.id=chatcmpl-B9x2 gen_ai.usage.input_tokens=1834 gen_ai.usage.output_tokens=212 gen_ai.response.finish_reasons=STOP gen_ai.output.messages="[content 980 chars #9c41d2e7]"
```

- **A whole agent turn** becomes one unit with `try (LOG.Unit turn = LOG.unit("agent-turn")) { ... }` around it: the calls of the model and the tools inside name it as `parent`, their warnings and errors count in it, and `LOG.wrap` carries it into the threads of the tools.
- **Prompts while debugging:** `-Dnanolog.content=show`, or a rule for the package of the listener such as `-Dnanolog.content.com.acme.ai=truncate:200`. With [`nanolog.buffer=DEBUG`](#breadcrumbs-debug-only-when-something-fails) the transcripts are written only before a failure.
- The field names follow the conventions, the values are what the frameworks report: the provider and the finish reason are enum names such as `OPEN_AI` and `STOP`, not the lower-case values of OpenTelemetry. With `JsonLogger` the fields are typed: `jq` sums `.fields["gen_ai.usage.input_tokens"]`.

## Context: tag the lines of one request

*Since 1.4.*

`LOG.context(key, value)` adds a pair to every entry the current thread logs until the scope is closed, so the lines of one request, job or test are found together, with `grep requestId=r-17` or by an agent reading the log:

```java
try (LOG.Context c = LOG.context("requestId", requestId)) {
    LOG.info("Charging {}", amount);
    // INFO 16.11.2026 10:15:02 [PaymentService] Charging 42 requestId=r-17

    executor.submit(LOG.wrap(() -> LOG.info("Sending the receipt")));
    // a thread of the pool logs it with requestId=r-17 as well
}
```

- `ConsoleLogger` prints the pairs after the message. A value that is empty or contains a space, a quote or `=` goes in double quotes, `user="John Smith"`, so every pair reads as one; `showContext=false` hides them.
- `JsonLogger` writes a nested object, `"context":{"requestId":"r-17"}`, which cannot collide with `level`, `message` and the other fields; numbers and booleans keep their JSON type.
- `Slf4jLogger` puts the pairs into the MDC while it forwards an entry and takes them out afterwards, so `%X{requestId}` prints them in Logback and Log4j 2.
- Every entry keeps its context as `LogEntry.getContext()`, so `MemoryLogger` assertions and custom loggers see it, and the assertion messages of `MemoryLogger` show it.
- Scopes nest: an inner scope adds a key or sets one again, and closing it puts the previous value back. Close each scope in the thread that opened it, as try-with-resources does.
- The context belongs to the thread. A pool thread does not inherit it, because it would inherit the context of the code that happened to create the thread. `LOG.wrap(task)` takes the context and the open unit of `LOG.unit(...)` when it is called, then runs the task with them in whatever thread and removes them when the task ends, also when it throws.
- As with `ExecutorService.submit`, a lambda that returns a value, `() -> list.add(item)`, is a `Callable` to the compiler; write `() -> { list.add(item); }` where a `Runnable` is needed.
- Every entry reads one `ThreadLocal`. A thread without a context keeps nothing in it, virtual threads included.

### Context providers

The trace ID of OpenTelemetry, of New Relic or of a request scope lives in a context of its own, not in `LOG.context`. A context provider adds such keys to every entry, without a dependency of Nanolog on that library:

```java
LOG.addContextProvider(() -> {
    SpanContext span = Span.current().getSpanContext();
    if (!span.isValid()) {
        return null;
    }
    Map<String, Object> ids = new LinkedHashMap<>();
    ids.put("traceId", span.getTraceId());
    ids.put("spanId", span.getSpanId());
    return ids;
});
```

- A provider is asked when an entry is created, in the thread that logs: only for an enabled level and once per entry, so keep it cheap. It may return `null` or an empty map; a `null` key is ignored.
- Its keys come after the pairs of `LOG.context`, which win over them, and a provider added earlier wins over a later one. They reach the loggers like the other pairs: `ConsoleLogger` prints `traceId=4bf92f35...` after the message, `JsonLogger` writes them into `"context"`, `Slf4jLogger` puts them into the MDC for `%X{traceId}`, and keys named like secrets are masked.
- A provider that throws is reported once with a `[NANOLOG]` line, and the entry is logged without its keys. An entry that a provider logs itself gets no keys from the providers.
- In the configuration, `nanolog.context.provider=com.acme.TraceIdProvider` names a class that implements `Supplier<Map<String, ?>>` and has a public no-argument constructor; several are separated by commas and come before the providers of `addContextProvider`. A class that cannot be created is reported and left out.
- Providers apply to the whole JVM and stay after `LOG.init()`; `LOG.removeContextProvider(provider)` removes one. A task of `LOG.wrap(task)` asks them in the thread that runs it, where OpenTelemetry has carried its own context.

## Rate limiting

A retry loop, a full queue or a deprecated option can print the same line thousands of times, and the line that matters scrolls away. `LOG.once()` and `LOG.atMostEvery(...)` limit one statement:

```java
LOG.once().warn("Option {} is deprecated and ignored", key);
LOG.atMostEvery(10, TimeUnit.SECONDS).warn("Queue is full, dropping {}", item);
// the next line that gets through says how many were skipped:
// WARN 16.11.2026 10:15:02 [Worker] Queue is full, dropping 17 [skipped 241]
```

- A statement is its call site, the file and line of the call. Two calls on one line share one limit, and so do all the callers of a helper method that logs for them, unless the helper is skipped: [Logging helpers](#logging-helpers).
- The next entry that gets through carries the number of calls skipped since the previous one: `ConsoleLogger` prints `[skipped 241]` after the message, `JsonLogger` writes `"skipped":241`, `Slf4jLogger` appends `[skipped 241]` to the message, and any logger reads `LogEntry.getSkippedCount()`.
- The level is checked first, the limit last: a call at a disabled level is not counted, and a skipped call builds no message and formats nothing.
- `once()` and `atMostEvery(...)` offer four shapes at every level: `("... {} ...", args)`, `(() -> message)` and both with an exception first. The state of each call site takes a few bytes and is updated without locks, and the number of call sites is bounded by the code.
- A count left at the end of a burst is printed only when the statement runs again. A period of zero or less limits nothing.

## Tags

*Since 1.4.*

Some entries belong to a concern rather than to a class: audit, security, SQL. `LOG.tag(name)` marks them, wherever they come from:

```java
LOG.tag("audit").warn("User {} changed role to {}", user, role);
LOG.tag("sql").debug("{} rows in {} ms", rows, millis);
```

```
WARN 18.11.2026 10:30:00 [UserService] [audit] User alice changed role to admin
```

- Levels per tag: `nanolog.tags=audit=WARN,sql=DEBUG` (`NANOLOG_TAGS`). A rule for the tag of an entry overrides the global level and the package rules, so the audit entries below `WARN` are dropped wherever they come from, and the SQL entries at `DEBUG` are written even under `nanolog.level=INFO`. A tag without a rule follows the level of its class. `resetLevels()` reads the rules again; `LOG.setLevel` does not change them.
- `ConsoleLogger` writes `[audit]` after the source class, `JsonLogger` `"tags":["audit"]`, and `Slf4jLogger` passes an SLF4J `Marker` named after the tag. Any logger reads `LogEntry.getTags()` and may answer `ILogger.isEnabled(level, sourceClass, tag)`; by default it ignores the tag.
- A tag has the four shapes of `LOG.once()` at every level: a message with arguments, a lazy message, and both with an exception first. `LOG.tag("audit").once()` and `.atMostEvery(...)` limit a tagged statement. An entry has at most one tag; `LOG.tag(null)` logs without one.
- A tag costs nothing over an ordinary call. A rule that enables a level for a tag, `sql=DEBUG` under `INFO`, makes the level possible, so every call at that level walks the stack, as a package rule does.

## Catching exceptions

*Since 1.4.*

Two patterns repeat in every code base: the `try { ... } catch (Exception e) { LOG.error(...) }` block that logs and carries on, and the exception that kills a background thread and is printed by the JVM as `Exception in thread "pool-1-thread-3"`, outside the log format, outside `JsonLogger` and out of sight of `MemoryLogger`:

```java
LOG.installUncaughtExceptionHandler(); // once, at startup: exceptions that kill threads go into the log

LOG.catching(() -> connection.close()); // best-effort cleanup: ERROR with the stack trace, then carry on
// ERROR 16.11.2026 10:15:02 [Catching] Caught and ignored
// java.io.IOException: Connection reset ...

int retries = LOG.catching(() -> Integer.parseInt(text), 3); // a default value when it fails
// ERROR 16.11.2026 10:15:02 [Catching] Caught, returning 3
// java.lang.NumberFormatException: For input string: "many" ...
```

- **When to swallow.** `LOG.catching` is for work whose failure must not stop the caller: closing a resource, deleting a temporary file, a best-effort notification or metric. Do not use it where the caller must know about the failure, such as saving data, charging, or anything whose result the next step relies on: let the exception propagate, or handle it.
- The exception is logged at `ERROR` with its stack trace, from the class and call site of the `LOG.catching` call, and the levels apply as usual. The actions may throw checked exceptions (`LOG.ThrowingRunnable`, `LOG.ThrowingSupplier`). An `Error` is not caught, and an `InterruptedException` is caught with the interrupt flag of the thread set again. Inside a [unit](#wide-events-one-line-per-request-canonical-log-lines) a caught exception makes the unit fail, like any `ERROR`.
- **Threads.** `LOG.installUncaughtExceptionHandler()` installs a default handler that logs `Uncaught exception in thread worker-1` with the stack trace, then passes the exception to the handler installed before, so test frameworks and existing handlers still see it; without one, the JVM no longer prints it itself. Installing again changes nothing.
- The entry of an uncaught exception has the class and call site of the first frame of its stack trace outside the JDK, the code that failed, not the dispatch code of the JVM. The dying thread first writes its [breadcrumbs](#breadcrumbs-debug-only-when-something-fails), then the exception, then its units still open, as `interrupted`.

## System.out and System.err

*Since 1.4.*

Libraries and old code print with `System.out.println` and `e.printStackTrace()`. Their lines have no level and no source, miss `JsonLogger` and are not captured by `MemoryLogger`. `LOG.captureSystemStreams()`, or `nanolog.captureSystemStreams=true`, makes each such line an entry:

```
INFO 18.11.2026 10:30:00 [LegacyImporter] Imported 120 rows
ERROR 18.11.2026 10:30:01 [LegacyImporter] java.io.IOException: disk full
```

- A line of `System.out` becomes an `INFO` entry, a line of `System.err` an `ERROR` entry; the levels apply, so a line at a disabled level is dropped. The source class and the call site are those of the code that printed; the frames of `PrintStream`, `printf` and `printStackTrace` are skipped.
- A line ends at `\n` or `\r\n`, or when the stream is flushed; a partial line waits, per thread, so the lines of two threads do not mix. Empty lines are dropped, and each line of a stack trace is an entry of its own. The text is kept whole whatever the charset of the platform.
- No loop: Nanolog writes its own output, the console included, to the streams it found when the capture started, and what a logger prints to `System.out` while it writes an entry passes straight through.
- `LOG.restoreSystemStreams()` puts the streams back, unless something replaced them since; capturing or restoring twice changes nothing.

## java.util.logging and System.Logger into Nanolog

*Since 1.4.*

Many libraries log through `java.util.logging`, and the JDK through `System.Logger`. Their lines come in another format on another stream and miss `JsonLogger` and `MemoryLogger`. `NanologHandler` turns their records into entries of Nanolog:

```java
NanologHandler.install();   // once, at startup
```

or in `logging.properties`:

```properties
handlers=com.nanolaba.logging.NanologHandler
```

- `install()` replaces the handlers of the root logger, its console handler among them, so nothing is printed twice; `uninstall()` puts them back. A record becomes an entry of the code that called JUL, with the call site and the exception; the message is formatted as JUL formats it, `{0}` parameters and resource bundles included.
- `SEVERE` becomes `ERROR`, `WARNING` `WARN`, `INFO` `INFO`, `CONFIG` and `FINE` `DEBUG`, `FINER` and `FINEST` `TRACE`; then the levels of Nanolog apply.
- JUL decides first: a record below the level of its JUL logger, `INFO` by default, never reaches Nanolog. To see the `FINE` records of one library, lower its level in JUL too, `com.zaxxer.hikari.level=FINE`; lowering the level of the root logger instead makes JUL build a record for every disabled call of every library.
- `System.Logger` (Java 9+) reaches the handler as well: the JDK sends it to JUL while the module `java.logging` is present. Nanolog registers no `System.LoggerFinder` of its own, which would take over `System.Logger` in every application that has Nanolog on its classpath.
- Not together with `JulLogger`: entries would go round from Nanolog to JUL and back. A record that comes back is dropped, with one `[NANOLOG]` line.

## Caller detection

When no class is passed explicitly, `LOG` walks the stack and takes the first frame
that does not belong to `LOG`, `LogEntry` or an `ILogger` implementation. On Java 9+ a
`StackWalker` does it and stops at that frame; on Java 8 `Reflection.getCallerClass` gives the class of each frame.

- Nested, anonymous and lambda classes are attributed to their top-level enclosing class.
- The frame found by the walk is kept as `LogEntry.getCaller()`: the exact class, method, file and line of the call, including nested classes and lambdas. It costs nothing extra, and it is `null` when the class was passed explicitly.
- On Java 9+ the stack walker hands over the class of each frame, so the caller is found exactly whatever class loader it lives in. On Java 8 the internal `sun.reflect.Reflection.getCallerClass(int)` does the same, and only the frames up to the caller become `StackTraceElement`s (`JavaLangAccess.getStackTraceElement`); where the two disagree, under `Method.invoke`, the call falls back to the stack trace of a `Throwable`. Where neither is available (another JVM, a native image without the metadata for `StackWalker`), the frames of a `Throwable` carry only class names: they are resolved through the context class loader of the thread first and the class loader of `LOG` second, so the detection works when Nanolog lives in a shared loader of an application server and the caller in a web application. A frame neither loader can see or load is skipped, whatever the failure: a missing class, a linkage error such as `NoClassDefFoundError`, or `MissingReflectionRegistrationError` from GraalVM in a native image.
- The stack is walked only for a level the logger may have enabled: `LOG` first asks `ILogger.mayBeEnabled(level)`, so a level that is off for every class, such as `DEBUG` under `nanolog.level=INFO`, costs no walk. `LOG.isDebugEnabled()` follows the same rule. Once a level is on anywhere, even for one package (`nanolog.level.com.acme.db=TRACE`), every call at that level walks the stack, because only the class tells whether it is enabled. In hot paths pass the class explicitly: `LOG.debug(MyClass.class, ...)`.
- Any class implementing `ILogger` is skipped, so a custom logger that logs through `LOG` must pass its source class explicitly.
- If no frame qualifies, the entry is still logged, without a source class and a call site, as with `LOG.log(level, null, ...)`. That happens when the code runs entirely inside an `ILogger` class, or on Java 8 when the JVM records no stack traces (`-XX:-StackTraceInThrowable`). `Slf4jLogger` sends such entries to the `ROOT` logger.

### Logging helpers

*Since 1.4.*

A helper that logs for others, such as an `Audit.record(...)` method or a base class of tasks, would be the source of every entry it logs, and its callers would share one rate limit of `LOG.once()`. Name such helpers in `nanolog.caller.skip` (or `NANOLOG_CALLER_SKIP`), class or package names separated by commas:

```properties
nanolog.caller.skip=com.acme.Audit,com.acme.logging
```

- Their frames are skipped like those of `LOG`: the entry gets the source class, the call site and the rate limit of the code that called the helper.
- A class covers its nested classes, and a package its classes and subpackages, by whole segments of the name: `com.acme.log` does not cover `com.acme.logging`. A nested class alone is written with `$`, `com.acme.Outer$Helper`.
- A library that wraps `LOG` cannot rely on the settings of the application: it calls `LOG.skipCaller(Helper.class)` once, for example in a static initializer. These classes are added to those named in the setting and stay skipped after `LOG.init()`.
- `Slf4jLogger` passes the helper to a location-aware backend as the caller boundary, so `%file:%line` of Logback and `%l` of Log4j 2 point at the code that called the helper as well.
- The match is found once per class and cached, so a skipped helper adds no string comparison to later calls. An invalid name, such as `com.acme.*`, prints a `[NANOLOG]` diagnostic and is left out; when every frame is skipped, the entry is logged without a source class, as above.

## Writing your own logger

`ILogger` has a single abstract method, so the simplest implementation is a lambda:

```java
LOG.init(entry -> System.out.println(
        entry.getLevel() + " [" + entry.getSourceClass().getSimpleName() + "] " + entry.getFormattedMessage()));
```

A full implementation also filters levels:

```java
public class CustomLogger implements ILogger {

    @Override
    public void log(LogEntry entry) {
        // write the entry wherever you need: a file, a socket, a queue, ...
        System.out.println(entry.getLevel() + " " + entry.getFormattedMessage());
    }

    @Override
    public boolean isEnabled(LogEntry.LogEntryLevel level, Class sourceClass) {
        // called before the LogEntry is built and before any Supplier is evaluated:
        // return false to suppress entries of this level for this class
        return level != LogEntry.LogEntryLevel.TRACE;
    }

    @Override
    public boolean mayBeEnabled(LogEntry.LogEntryLevel level) {
        // asked before the source class is detected: false spares the stack walk too,
        // so return false only for a level that isEnabled rejects for every class
        return level != LogEntry.LogEntryLevel.TRACE;
    }
}
```

What a `LogEntry` carries:

- `getLevel()` — `TRACE`, `DEBUG`, `INFO`, `WARN` or `ERROR`.
- `getSourceClass()` — the detected or explicitly passed class; `null` only if `null` was passed.
- `getCaller()` — the `StackTraceElement` of the logging call; `null` when the source class was passed explicitly.
- `getThrowable()` — the exception or `null`.
- `getMessage()` — the raw message object, already resolved from its `Supplier`.
- `getTimestamp()`, `getThreadName()` — when and in which thread the entry was created, so a logger that writes later or elsewhere still knows.
- `getArgs()` — the substitution arguments.
- `isDbg()`, `isBreadcrumb()` — whether the entry comes from `LOG.dbg`, and whether `nanolog.buffer` held it back.
- `getFields()`, `getTrailingFields()` — the arguments of `LOG.kv(...)` by name, and those of them that no `{}` took.
- `getContext()` — the pairs of `LOG.context(...)` open in the thread that created the entry; an empty map without them.
- `getFormattedMessage()` — the final string with `{}` substituted.

`isEnabled(...)` is called before the `LogEntry` is built and before any `Supplier` is resolved, so returning `false` skips the whole cost of the message. It does not skip caller detection: for a call without an explicit class the source class is found first, so the stack has already been walked; see [Caller detection](#caller-detection).

To spare the walk as well, override `mayBeEnabled(level)`, as the example above does: `LOG` asks it before caller detection, and `false` means that no class has the level enabled. The default `true` is always safe; `false` for a level that `isEnabled(...)` accepts for some class loses those entries. `ConsoleLogger`, `JsonLogger` and `CompositeLogger` implement it; a subclass that overrides `isEnabled(...)` but not `mayBeEnabled(...)` gets `true`.

A logger that throws does not break the code that logs. The first failure of each logger class prints one line to `System.err`, for example `[NANOLOG] Logger com.acme.AuditLogger threw java.io.UncheckedIOException: disk full; entries it fails to write are printed to System.err`. Every entry the logger fails to write then goes to `System.err` in the `ConsoleLogger` format, so nothing is lost. If `isEnabled(...)` throws, the level counts as enabled.

## Thread safety and performance

- The static `LOG` methods are safe to call from any thread as long as the installed `ILogger` is; `ConsoleLogger` and `Slf4jLogger` are.
- A logger installed with `LOG.init(...)` or `MemoryLogger.install()` is used by every thread from its next logging call, threads that are already running included. Levels may change at any time, through `LOG.setLevel(...)` and the other level methods or the level setters of `ConsoleLogger`. The display setters (`setShowDate`, `setDateFormat` and the others) are meant for startup, not for concurrent reconfiguration.
- A call at a level that is off for every class costs one `mayBeEnabled` check, or one `isEnabled` check with an explicit class. If a level is on for some package or class, a call at that level without an explicit class costs one stack walk and an `isEnabled` check even where the level is off, so a single rule such as `nanolog.level.com.acme.db=TRACE` makes every `trace` call without a class walk the stack. Message formatting and `Supplier` evaluation happen only for enabled levels.
- Measured with JMH on JDK 17 (Ryzen 5 5600X, Windows 10): a call at a level that is off for every class takes about 2 ns without a class and 7 ns with one. The stack walk, the price of a call without a class at a level enabled for some class, takes about 2.5 µs near the top of the stack and 3 µs at 100 frames; Java 8, which has no `StackWalker`, needs about 5 µs and 8 µs. An enabled line through `ConsoleLogger` takes under 1 µs, plus the walk if the class is not given. Other JDKs and the method: [src/jmh/RESULTS.md](src/jmh/RESULTS.md).

¹⁹ Nanolog: `FileLogger` rolls over by size only, with backups; no rolling by date, no compression, no asynchronous writing.<br>
²⁰ minlog: a category string in each call.<br>
²¹ tinylog 2: to java.util.logging and JBoss Logging, and a writer to Logcat; not to SLF4J (`slf4j-tinylog` goes the other way).<br>
²² minlog: a subclass of `Log.Logger`, set with `Log.setLogger`.<br>
²³ Nanolog: a level that is off for every class costs about 2 ns; a level enabled for another package walks the stack, about 3 µs on JDK 17 and 5 µs on Java 8, unless the class is passed.<br>
²⁴ tinylog: with levels per package, a disabled call between the global level and the most verbose package level looks up the caller first.<br>
²⁵ Timber: `DebugTree` takes the tag from a new stack trace before `isLoggable`.

### Mainstream loggers

The loggers most Java code already uses, and Flogger, which limits the rate per call site.

### Next to tinylog 2.8.1

tinylog is the closest analogue. The same calls, run on Java 8 with the default configuration of both:

| Call | tinylog 2.8.1 | Nanolog |
|---|---|---|
| `error("failed {}", id, e)` | the message only, the stack trace is dropped | the message and the stack trace |
| `info("{\"id\": {}}", 42)` | `"id": {}42` | `{"id": 42}` |
| `info("{foo} and {}", "bar")` | a warning, then `bar and {}` | `{foo} and bar` |
| an argument whose `toString()` throws | the exception reaches the caller | `[FAILED toString()]` |
| changing the configuration after the first log call | `UnsupportedOperationException` | `LOG.init` and `LOG.setLevel` at any time |
| packaging | api and impl jars, found by ServiceLoader | one jar |
| Java baseline of the next major version | tinylog 3, not released yet, drops Java 8 | Java 8 |

When ServiceLoader does not find `tinylog-impl`, nothing is logged: [#126](https://github.com/tinylog-org/tinylog/issues/126), [#135](https://github.com/tinylog-org/tinylog/issues/135), [#140](https://github.com/tinylog-org/tinylog/issues/140). Java 8 in tinylog 3: [#398](https://github.com/tinylog-org/tinylog/issues/398).

### When another logger fits better

- **Log files in production with rolling by date.** Rolling by time, compression and retention by age: Logback, Log4j 2, tinylog. `FileLogger` of Nanolog rolls over by size only.
- **Asynchronous output and high throughput.** The asynchronous appenders and loggers of Logback and Log4j 2, the writing thread of tinylog.
- **An ecosystem.** Appenders for syslog, databases, message queues and log services, markers and filters, the configuration of Spring Boot: SLF4J with Logback or Log4j 2. Nanolog can write through them with [`Slf4jLogger`](#slf4jlogger).
- **Android.** Timber writes to Logcat and checks its format strings with Android Lint. Nanolog is not tested on Android.

## Changelog

### 1.4

- Agent mode: when the environment names a coding agent (`AI_AGENT`, `AGENT`, `CLAUDECODE`, `GEMINI_CLI`, `CODEX_SANDBOX`, `CODEX_CI`, `CURSOR_AGENT`, `VSCODE_AGENT`, `CLINE_ACTIVE`), the console of the default logger shows `WARN` and above, one line per entry, without dates or colours and with short stack traces, `LOG.dbg` prints whatever the levels, the run log is on, and one `[NANOLOG]` line says so and names the file. `nanolog.agent=auto|on|off` decides; an explicitly set level or display setting wins.
- Documentation: what agent mode saves, measured in tokens. Four runs of a small project in `src/tokens`, with the script that repeats them; a failing test run printed 1,022 tokens instead of 13,577 (o200k_base). See [Fewer tokens](#fewer-tokens-logs-for-ai-coding-agents).
- Run summary, `nanolog.summary=on|off|errors`, on by default in agent mode: the run ends with the counts by level, each kind of warning and error with its call site and count, the trace of the first error, the `LOG.dbg` calls that ran and the path of the run log. The summary is printed last so that it survives when an agent keeps only the tail of the output. In test runs `SummaryListener`, which the JUnit Platform loads by itself, prints it and the list of `LOG.dbg` calls when the tests have run, because Surefire drops what a shutdown hook of its forked JVM prints.
- Run log for agents: with `nanolog.run=on` every entry of the run also goes to `target/nanolog/latest.log` (Gradle: `build/nanolog`, otherwise `.nanolog`), warnings and errors to `latest.errors.log` one line each, and the absolute path is printed when `LOG` initialises. Each run writes `runs/<time>-<pid>.log`, `latest.log` is a hard link to it, the last 10 runs are kept. `nanolog.run.dir`, `nanolog.run.format=json`, `nanolog.run.keep`, `nanolog.run.maxSize`.
- `LOG.dbg(expression)` prints the expression as written in the source, its value and type, and the call site, and returns the value; `LOG.dbg(a, b, ...)` prints several, `LOG.dbg()` that the line was reached. Without the source only the values are printed. `ConsoleLogger` marks the line `DBG`, `JsonLogger` adds `"dbg":true`, `LogEntry.isDbg()` tells the entry apart; `nanolog.sources` names the source directories.
- Objects whose class has no `toString()` of its own are printed field by field instead of `Invoice@2f92e0f4`: always in `LOG.dbg`, and in `{}` arguments with `nanolog.dump=auto`. Classes of the JDK are never reflected into, so nothing needs `--add-opens` on JDK 17+; cycles, depth, items and string length are limited, and every cut says what it left out; fields named like secrets print `***`; records show their components, proxies only their class name.
- Leftover `LOG.dbg` calls: when the JVM exits, one `[NANOLOG]` line lists the call sites that printed; `nanolog.dbg=off` silences the calls, `nanolog.dbg=fail` reports each one as a diagnostic that fails `MemoryLogger.assertNoDiagnostics()`; `NanologChecks.assertNoDbgCalls("src/main/java")` fails a test while the sources call `LOG.dbg`, with the file, line and code of each call. `MemoryLogger.assertNoDiagnostics()` now says `Nanolog reported` instead of `strict mode reported`.
- Wide events: `LOG.unit("checkout")` opens a unit of work that writes one canonical log line per request or job when it closes, `checkout ok 182 ms orderId=A-17 warn=1`: the outcome (`ok`, `error`, `interrupted`), the duration, the fields of `put(...)`, the counts of warnings and errors logged inside it and, for a failed unit, `error.type`, `error.message` and an `error.key` that stays the same between runs. Units nest (`parent=`), cross executors with `LOG.wrap` and are written as `interrupted` when the run ends while they are open; `nanolog.unit.sample` / `nanolog.unit.slowMs` sample the fast successful ones; `run(...)` and `LOG.unit(name, body)` record a thrown exception.
- Settings that Nanolog does not know are reported when `LOG` initialises instead of being ignored: a mistyped `nanolog.*` system property, `NANOLOG_*` environment variable or key of `nanolog.properties` prints `[NANOLOG] Unknown setting "nanolog.levle" (system property); did you mean "nanolog.level"?`, a key of the file without the `nanolog.` prefix is reported as ignored, and `NANOLOG_LEVEL_COM_ACME` points to `NANOLOG_LEVELS`. Keys of a custom logger under a namespace of its own are left alone.
- `NanologExtension`, a JUnit 5 extension: the log of a test is held back and printed only when the test fails, framed by `--- log of PaymentServiceTest.chargeIsRetried ---`; a passing or aborted test writes it only to the run log. Parallel tests keep their logs apart, and `nanolog.junit.output=failed|all|none` decides what is printed.
- `nanolog.console.multiline` (`setMultiline`) for `ConsoleLogger`: `indent` starts every line of an entry after the first with a tab, so a message cannot forge an entry; `escape` writes line breaks as `\r` and `\n`, so an entry and its stack trace are one physical line; both write other control characters, terminal escape sequences among them, as `\u001b`. `keep`, the default, changes nothing; agent mode uses `escape`.
- Coloured level words on a terminal, `nanolog.console.color=auto|always|never` (`setColor`): red `ERROR`, yellow `WARN`, green `INFO`, dim `DEBUG` and `TRACE`, magenta `DBG`. `auto`, the default, colours only when standard output is a terminal, honours `NO_COLOR`, `FORCE_COLOR` and `TERM=dumb`, and stays off on Windows and in agent mode; pipes, files, the run log and `JsonLogger` never get escape codes.
- `java.util.logging` both ways: `JulLogger` (`nanolog.logger=com.nanolaba.logging.JulLogger`) writes the entries to JUL, to the logger of the source class with the call site, and asks JUL for the levels; `NanologHandler.install()` or `handlers=com.nanolaba.logging.NanologHandler` turns the records of JUL, and so of `System.Logger`, into entries of the code that called it. A loop between the two is reported and cut.
- GraalVM native image and Android: the jar carries the metadata of a native image (`META-INF/native-image`: the constructors of the loggers, the stack walker, `nanolog.properties`) and rules for R8 and ProGuard (`META-INF/proguard/nanolog.pro`), so neither needs setup; CI builds and runs a native image on GraalVM 21 and 25.
- `FileLogger`: `nanolog.logger=com.nanolaba.logging.FileLogger` with `nanolog.file=logs/app.log` appends the entries to a file, in the text format of `ConsoleLogger` or the JSON lines of `JsonLogger`. Each entry is written through at once, or with `nanolog.file.flush=buffer` kept until `LOG.flush()`; the file rolls over at `nanolog.file.maxSize`, with `nanolog.file.backups`. `LOG.flush()` and `ILogger.flush()` are new.
- A real module descriptor: on Java 9+ the jar is the module `com.nanolaba.nanolog`, from `META-INF/versions/9/module-info.class` of a multi-release jar, so `jlink` accepts it; the module needs only `java.base`.
- `LOG.captureSystemStreams()` and `nanolog.captureSystemStreams=true` turn the lines printed to `System.out` and `System.err` into `INFO` and `ERROR` entries with the source and call site of the code that printed, `e.printStackTrace()` included, without a loop through the console.
- Calls from Kotlin are checked: CI compiles the calls of `LOG` in every form from Kotlin, so an overload that is ambiguous for Kotlin, as in tinylog, fails the build.
- `Slf4jLogger` is tested against SLF4J 1.7 as well as 2.x: CI runs the tests once more with slf4j-api and slf4j-simple 1.7.36.
- A library that replaces the logger of the application is reported: when code of another organization (the first two segments of the package) replaces a logger installed with `LOG.init(logger)`, a `[NANOLOG]` line names both call sites. `LOG.lock()` and `nanolog.logger.lock=true` keep the installed logger and turn later `LOG.init` calls into no-ops with such a line; `MemoryLogger.install()` still works under the lock.
- Documentation: a `nanolog.properties` in `src/test/resources` replaces the one in `src/main/resources` in tests, as a whole file, not merged.
- Several `nanolog.properties` on the classpath, at least one of them in a jar, are reported with one `[NANOLOG]` line that lists them and names the one that was read: a library that ships its own file no longer wins over the file of the application without a word. Two directories, such as the main and the test resources, stay quiet.
- Tags: `LOG.tag("audit").warn(...)` marks the entries of a concern rather than of a class, and `nanolog.tags=audit=WARN,sql=DEBUG` sets levels per tag, which take precedence over the levels of the class. `ConsoleLogger` writes `[audit]`, `JsonLogger` `"tags":["audit"]`, `Slf4jLogger` passes an SLF4J `Marker`; `LogEntry.getTags()` and `ILogger.isEnabled(level, sourceClass, tag)` are new.
- Lazy arguments: `LOG.debug("Stats: {}", LOG.lazy(() -> summarize(stats)))` computes one argument only if the level is enabled, once, and keeps the template for strict mode, `JsonLogger` and `assertTemplateLogged`.
- `nanolog.console.sourceLength` (`setSourceLength`) abbreviates a fully qualified source name like `%logger{n}` of Logback: `com.acme.billing.payments.PaymentService` becomes `c.a.b.p.PaymentService` at 20 characters.
- `nanolog.console.timeZone` (`setTimeZone`) sets the time zone of the `ConsoleLogger` timestamps, such as `UTC` or `Europe/Berlin`; an unknown ID is reported instead of being taken for GMT. `nanolog.console.dateFormat=iso` stands for the ISO 8601 pattern with milliseconds and the offset of the zone.
- Context providers: `LOG.addContextProvider(() -> ids)` and `nanolog.context.provider=com.acme.TraceIdProvider` add the keys of a context of their own, such as the trace ID of OpenTelemetry, to every entry, after the pairs of `LOG.context`, which win. A provider is asked only for an enabled entry; one that throws is reported once and the entry is logged without its keys.
- Logging helpers: `nanolog.caller.skip=com.acme.Audit,com.acme.logging` and `LOG.skipCaller(Helper.class)` skip the frames of classes and packages that log for others, so an entry logged through `Audit.record(...)` gets the source class, call site and rate limit of the code that called the helper, and `Slf4jLogger` passes the helper to Logback and Log4j 2 as the caller boundary.
- Strict mode reports two more mistakes, with the call site: an argument that repeats the message of the exception logged with it, `LOG.error("Failed: {}", e.getMessage(), e)`, and a call site seen with two different templates, that is, a template built from data, such as `LOG.info("User " + id + " from {}", ip)`. Like the placeholder check, both reach `ILogger.onDiagnostic` and fail `MemoryLogger.assertNoDiagnostics()`; calls without arguments are not checked.
- README: *Related projects*, a comparison with tinylog, jcabi-log, minlog, Timber, SLF4J with Logback, Log4j 2, java.util.logging, Flogger and JBoss Logging, with the calls that behave differently in tinylog.
- Faster caller detection on Java 8: `Reflection.getCallerClass` gives the class of each frame and only the frames up to the caller are built, so a call without a class at a level enabled for some class costs about 5 µs instead of 20 near the top of the stack and 19 µs instead of 270 at 500 frames; the stack trace of a `Throwable` stays the fallback.
- Secrets: `LOG.secret(token)` is written as `***` by every logger and keeps no value; fields and context values whose key names a secret, `password`, `token`, `apikey` and the others of `nanolog.redact`, are masked when the entry is created; a shown `LOG.content` masks keys of model providers, AWS keys, bearer tokens and JSON web tokens.
- `LOG.time("Load users")` and `LOG.timed("Count users", () -> ...)` time a block: `Load users took 123 ms` with the fields `timer` and `duration_ms`; a level that is off reads no clock, and the lambda form reports and rethrows an exception.
- `nanolog.console.repeats=collapse` (`setRepeats`), the default in agent mode: consecutive repeats of an entry become one line with a count, `(repeated 41 more times in 20.3 s)`, written when another entry comes, the logger is replaced or the run ends, and every ten seconds while the repeats go on; the run log, `JsonLogger` and `MemoryLogger` keep every entry.
- `nanolog.diagnostics=once|all|off`: each distinct `[NANOLOG]` diagnostic is printed once per JVM by default, configuration mistakes and the findings of strict mode at each call site included, so a `ConsoleLogger` created again does not repeat them; `all` prints every one, `off` none. A diagnostic about an invalid value says where it was set: a system property, an environment variable or the file. The run summary and the other notices are not affected.
- `nanolog.console.showSourceLine` (`setShowSourceLine`): the source line of the call under each entry, `    > LOG.warn("Charge of {} failed", amount);`, and under the first three frames of a stack trace outside the JDK. The line is found as `LOG.dbg` finds its source and left out when the source is missing or stale; `JsonLogger` adds `"source"` to `"caller"`. A part of a `ConsoleLogger` line that follows a line break no longer starts with a space.
- `LOG.catching(() -> cleanup())` logs an exception at `ERROR` with its stack trace and carries on, `LOG.catching(() -> parse(s), -1)` returns a default instead; checked exceptions are allowed, an `Error` is not caught, an interruption is kept. `LOG.installUncaughtExceptionHandler()` logs the exceptions that kill threads, from the first frame outside the JDK, then passes them to the previous handler; the dying thread writes its breadcrumbs and its open units too.
- README: *Logging LLM calls*, a LangChain4j listener and a Spring AI advisor that log one line per model call with the OpenTelemetry `gen_ai.*` field names, the prompt and the completion as `LOG.content`, and a transcript at `DEBUG`.
- Payloads: `LOG.content(prompt)` writes a prompt, a response or a request body as `[content 1834 chars #3f2a9c1b]`, its length and a hash keyed per JVM, unless `nanolog.content=truncate:<characters>` or `show` says otherwise, for all classes or, through `nanolog.content.<package or class>`, for some. The text is taken when the entry is created and always escaped against forged lines; in JSON fields a hidden payload is `{"content_len":1834,"content_hash":"3f2a9c1b"}`.
- Breadcrumbs: `nanolog.buffer=DEBUG` holds `DEBUG` and `TRACE` entries back, the newest 200 per thread (`nanolog.buffer.size`), and writes them before the next `ERROR` under `--- 37 earlier DEBUG entries ---`; inside `LOG.unit` the unit drops them when it succeeds and writes them after its line when it fails. Held-back levels count as enabled, entries are snapshots with the time of their call, and `JsonLogger` marks them `"breadcrumb":true`.
- Fields: `LOG.kv("orderId", id)` names an argument. In a `{}` it prints its value; without one `ConsoleLogger` and `Slf4jLogger` append `orderId=A-17` to the message and strict mode does not count it. `JsonLogger` writes every field into a `"fields"` object whose numbers and booleans keep their type, so `jq` selects entries by them, and `LogEntry.getFields()` gives them to any logger.
- Context: `try (LOG.Context c = LOG.context("requestId", id)) { ... }` adds `requestId=r-17` to every entry the thread logs inside the block, nested scopes put the previous value back, and `LOG.wrap(task)` carries the context into a task that another thread runs. `ConsoleLogger` prints the pairs after the message (`nanolog.console.showContext`), `JsonLogger` writes a `"context"` object whose numbers and booleans keep their type, `Slf4jLogger` puts the pairs into the MDC for `%X{requestId}`, and `LogEntry.getContext()` gives them to any logger.
- `MemoryLogger.capture()` and `captureForwarding()` capture the entries of the current thread only, every level, while the logger of `LOG` stays installed for the other threads, so tests that run in parallel in one JVM can assert on their own log. The findings of strict mode on that thread reach the capture as well.

### 1.3

- Levels change while the application runs, thread-safely: `LOG.setLevel(level)`, `LOG.setLevel(name, level)`, `LOG.clearLevel(name)`, `LOG.resetLevels()`, and `LOG.withLevel(name, level)` for a `try` block. The level is a `LogEntryLevel` or a string such as `"OFF"`, as in the settings. `ConsoleLogger`, `JsonLogger` and `CompositeLogger` implement the new `ILevelControl`, and the level setters of `ConsoleLogger` may now be called while other threads log.
- `LOG.once()` and `LOG.atMostEvery(period, unit)` limit a statement to its first call or to one entry per period, keyed by the call site. The next entry that gets through carries the number of skipped calls, `LogEntry.getSkippedCount()`, which `ConsoleLogger`, `JsonLogger` and `Slf4jLogger` print.
- Shorter stack traces in `ConsoleLogger` and `JsonLogger`: `nanolog.exception.exclude` collapses runs of frames from packages such as `org.junit` or `jdk.internal.reflect` into `... N frames excluded`, `nanolog.exception.maxFrames` caps the frames of each throwable. Without them the output is that of `printStackTrace`, as before.
- `MemoryLogger`: `assertNoneAtOrAbove(level)`, `assertLogged(level, text)` and `assertTemplateLogged(level, template)` fail with an `AssertionError` that lists every captured entry, stack traces and call sites included; `getEntries(Class)` selects the entries of one source class.
- Strict mode reaches tests: every finding also goes to the installed logger through the new `ILogger.onDiagnostic`, every occurrence rather than the first one of a template, and `MemoryLogger.assertNoDiagnostics()` fails on them. `CompositeLogger` forwards them.
- `ConsoleLogger`, `JsonLogger`: `nanolog.console.stream` (or `setStream`) chooses the stream of each level: `out` sends everything to standard output, so `java -jar app.jar | jq` keeps the `ERROR` lines, `err` sends everything to standard error, `err@WARN` warnings and errors. The default `err@ERROR` is the former behaviour.
- `ConsoleLogger`: `setShowThread(true)` or `nanolog.console.showThread=true` prints the name of the thread after the date, `INFO 16.11.2026 10:15:02 [main] [PaymentService] Charged 42`. Off by default, so the format of existing output does not change.
- Calls without an explicit class no longer walk the stack when their level is off for every class: `LOG` asks the new `ILogger.mayBeEnabled(level)` first. `ConsoleLogger`, `JsonLogger` and `CompositeLogger` answer it from their switches, package rules and delegates; other loggers keep the default `true` and work as before.
- On Java 9+ caller detection uses `StackWalker`: it stops at the calling frame and loads no class by name, so a call without an explicit class costs about 3 µs instead of 9 to 26 µs on JDK 17 and hardly grows with the depth of the stack. A caller in a class loader that neither the context loader nor the loader of Nanolog can see is now found exactly instead of being skipped. Java 8 keeps the `Throwable` walk.
- A logger that throws no longer breaks the logging call: the failure is reported once per logger class with a `[NANOLOG]` line, and the entry is printed to `System.err` instead. Inside `CompositeLogger` a throwing delegate no longer stops the others.
- A lazy message whose `Supplier` throws no longer escapes from the logging call: the entry is logged with the message `[FAILED supplier: <exception>]`.
- When no stack frame qualifies as the caller (`-XX:-StackTraceInThrowable`, or code running entirely inside an `ILogger`), the entry is logged without a source class instead of throwing `IllegalStateException`.
- Caller detection no longer lets an error from a class loader escape: a frame whose class fails to load with `NoClassDefFoundError`, `MissingReflectionRegistrationError` from GraalVM or any other throwable is resolved through the other loader or skipped.
- A logger installed with `LOG.init(...)` or `MemoryLogger.install()` is now guaranteed to be seen by threads that are already logging; before, a test could miss entries logged from an executor thread.
- `ConsoleLogger`: an anonymous or local source class passed explicitly is printed as `[Foo$1]` instead of `[]` or `[null]`; `LogEntry.toString()` names it too.
- A `[NANOLOG]` diagnostic is always one line. Control characters in the values it repeats, such as a level passed to `LOG.setLevel` from a request, an exception message or a template, are printed as `\u000a` escapes, so such a value cannot forge a line of the log.
- Documentation: the `Slf4jLogger` section no longer says that MDC works with every backend; slf4j-simple and slf4j-nop discard MDC values.
- Documentation: `ILogger.isEnabled` no longer promises that returning `false` skips the whole cost of a call; caller detection has already walked the stack by then.
- JMH benchmarks in `src/jmh`, built with `mvn -P benchmark test-compile exec:exec`, with results for JDK 8 to 25 in [`src/jmh/RESULTS.md`](src/jmh/RESULTS.md); the README quotes the measured costs.

### 1.2

- A trailing `Throwable` that no `{}` consumes becomes the exception of the entry, as in SLF4J: `LOG.error("Failed", e)` and `LOG.error("Failed {}", id, e)` no longer drop the stack trace.
- `LogEntry.getCaller()` returns the frame of the logging call, and `ConsoleLogger.setShowLocation(true)` prints it as `[PaymentService.charge(PaymentService.java:87)]`.
- `ConsoleLogger` reads its levels and options from properties and environment variables: `nanolog.level`, `nanolog.level.<package or class>`, `nanolog.levels` and `nanolog.console.*`. Every property, `nanolog.logger` and `nanolog.config` included, can be set as an environment variable (`NANOLOG_LEVEL`), which beats `nanolog.properties`.
- `JsonLogger` writes one JSON object per line. `LogEntry.getTimestamp()` and `LogEntry.getThreadName()` tell when and where an entry was created.
- `MemoryLogger` captures entries in tests (`try (MemoryLogger log = MemoryLogger.install()) { ... }`), `CompositeLogger` sends entries to several loggers.
- `nanolog.strict=true` reports calls whose `{}` placeholders and arguments do not match, once per template, with the call site.
- `Slf4jLogger`: location-aware backends (Logback, Log4j 2) report the code that called `LOG` in `%file:%line` and `%l`, instead of `Slf4jLogger.log`.
- `ConsoleLogger`: a throwable whose `toString()` throws no longer escapes from the logging call; it is printed as `[FAILED printStackTrace()]`.
- The whole public API has Javadoc, and the build fails on a missing comment.
- [`llms.txt`](llms.txt) and the agent skill [`skills/nanolog/SKILL.md`](skills/nanolog/SKILL.md) give coding agents the rules of the library; both are generated with the README.

### 1.1

- New overloads `LOG.info(throwable, "... {} ...", args)` and `LOG.info(sourceClass, throwable, "... {} ...", args)` for every level: an exception together with a parameterized message.
- `nanolog.properties`: only `nanolog.` keys are copied into system properties; other keys are ignored.
- `Slf4jLogger`: a `null` source class goes to the `ROOT` logger instead of throwing; an entry without a message no longer logs the word `null`.
- Caller detection resolves classes through the context class loader first and skips frames it cannot see, instead of failing in application servers and plugin frameworks.
- `ConsoleLogger`: timestamp formatting is thread-safe.
- A broken `toString()` inside an `Object[]` argument no longer propagates to the caller.
- A `null` context class loader at startup is tolerated.
- The diagnostic for a missing configuration file names the right property.
- The jar declares `Automatic-Module-Name: com.nanolaba.nanolog`.

### 1.0

First release.
